metadata.title: Where Americans Work: The Jobs Race Since 1960
metadata.section: Section C: Labor Dynamics, Wages & Consumer Prices

events.label: Health care jobs pass factory jobs
Recession: 2 million factory jobs lost since 2007
Restaurants and hotels lose 7.8 million jobs

explanation.summary: Where Americans work has changed completely since 1960. Factory jobs peaked in 1979 and never came back. Health care grew almost tenfold and is now the largest of these sectors by far. Restaurants and hotels grew steadily, then lost half their jobs in a few weeks in 2020.
explanation.methodology: Payroll jobs by industry from the BLS Current Employment Statistics: health care and social assistance (CES6500000001), manufacturing (CES3000000001), leisure and hospitality (CES7000000001), construction (CES2000000001) and information (CES5000000001, which covers publishing, telecom, broadcasting and software publishing).

key_findings.title: 1979: The Factory Peak
key_findings.description: Manufacturing employed 19.55 million Americans, the most ever. As of September 2026 it employs 12.65 million.
key_findings.significance: About 7 million factory jobs have disappeared since 1979.

key_findings.title: 2001: Health Care Passes Factories
key_findings.description: Health care and social assistance jobs (about 15.9 million) passed manufacturing for the first time.
key_findings.significance: The US economy shifted from making things to caring for people.

key_findings.title: April 2020: Restaurants and Hotels Collapse
key_findings.description: Leisure and hospitality jobs fell to 8.7 million, from 16.5 million a year earlier. By 2026 they were back to about 17 million. Health care now employs 28.0 million.
key_findings.significance: The fastest job loss for any sector on record, and one of the fastest recoveries.
